questions.q: Where did the model card concept originate?
options: A 2018 Google research paper proposing short, standardized documents to accompany trained models
A government regulation requiring AI disclosure
Anthropic's original Responsible Scaling Policy
A requirement first introduced by the EU AI Act
questions.explain: "Model Cards for Model Reporting" (2018) proposed compact, standardized disclosure documents, originally for narrower single-purpose models.

questions.q: What is the main practical difference between a narrower model card and a modern frontier-model system card?
options: A system card is shorter and less detailed than a model card
A system card is a broader, release-specific document covering capabilities, safety evaluations, and mitigations for an entire model release
There is no real difference; the terms are perfectly interchangeable across every lab
A model card is only used for image classifiers and never for language models
questions.explain: System cards expanded the original, more compact model-card format into longer documents covering an entire frontier-model release, including dedicated safety evaluation sections.

questions.q: Besides external accountability, what internal effect does the practice of publishing a system card tend to have?
options: It eliminates the need for internal safety evaluations
It acts as a forcing function that pushes teams to run more rigorous, specific evaluations, since vague or missing results become visible in the final document
It guarantees that a model has zero safety issues
It replaces the need for any red-teaming
questions.explain: Knowing that evaluation results will be published tends to improve the rigor of the underlying work, because a vague or absent result is visible once the card is written.

questions.q: What distinguishes a strong system card from a weak one, according to this lesson?
options: A strong card uses more marketing language about safety commitment
A strong card cites specific evaluation names and scores, states what was not tested, and honestly acknowledges known limitations
A strong card omits all limitations to avoid alarming users
A strong card is always longer regardless of content
questions.explain: A strong card reads like an engineering report with specific, checkable claims rather than generic safety language.

questions.q: Why does external accountability depend on a card's claims being specific rather than vague?
options: Because specific claims are always legally binding contracts
Because a specific, falsifiable claim can be scrutinized, replicated, or challenged by outside researchers and regulators, while a vague assurance cannot
Because vague claims are illegal under current law
Because specificity is only relevant to internal teams, not external parties
questions.explain: A card's value for outside accountability comes from making checkable claims; vague language gives outside parties nothing concrete to verify.
